This bill is part of a package that would bring back the Australian Building and Construction Commission (ABCC).
The package would replace the current industry regulator with a new body that has stronger powers and higher penalties for unlawful conduct in the building sector.
The explanatory memorandum says the package builds on two earlier Acts, but does not specify a start date for the changes.
Re-establishes the Australian Building and Construction Commission as the industry regulator.
Restores higher penalties for building industry participants who break industrial laws.
Introduces specific provisions on unlawful action and coercion in the building industry.
Participants in the building and construction industry, including employers, workers, and unions.

The majority voted to speed up the passage of the bills so that they could immediately vote on whether to pass it. In parliamentary jargon, they voted to suspend the [standing and sessional orders](http://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/standing-orders.html) that would have stopped the bills from being passed immediately (ordinarily, they couldn't be passed until the next sitting day). ### What were the bills about? The bills re-institute a workplace relations framework that was first put in place back in 2005. Among other things, they re-establish the [Australian Building and Construction Commissioner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_of_the_Australian_Building_and_Construction_Commissioner) and re-introduce provisions dealing with unlawful [industrial action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_action) and coercion that are specific to the building industry. Read more in the [bills digest](http://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1314a/14bd034).

The bill increases family tax benefit A by $10 per fortnight for some families and introduces a $1,000 annual payment for families with children under one, but cuts family tax benefit B for single parents with children aged 13–16 (by around $1,700–$3,100), abolishes it for single parents whose youngest child is 17–19 and in secondary school, and phases out end-of-year supplements over two years. The majority agreed with the main idea of the bill. In parliamentary jargon, they agreed to give the bill a [second reading](http://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). This means that the House can now discuss the bill in more detail. ### Bill's main idea The main idea of the bill is to undo some of the measures that haven't yet begun but were introduced under the previous Labor Government's 2013-14 Budget. That is, it repeals all the parts of the [Clean Energy (Income Tax Rates Amendments) Act 2011](https://www.comlaw.gov.au/Details/C2011A00150) and the [Clean Energy (Tax Laws Amendments) Act 2011](https://www.comlaw.gov.au/Details/C2011A00159) that were meant to begin at a future date. The bill doesn't repeal any parts of those two Acts that are already in operation. ### What exactly does the bill do? According to the [bills digest](http://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1415a/15bd026), the bill will: * "*repeal an increase in the nominal tax-free threshold from $18,200 in 2014–15 to $19,400 in 2015–16* * *maintain the second personal marginal tax rate at 32.5 per cent rather than increase it to 33 per cent from 2015–16* * *maintain the maximum value of the low income tax offset (**LITO**) at $445 rather than change the maximum value of the LITO to $300 from 2015–16 and* * *maintain the threshold below which a person may receive LITO at a taxable income of $66,667 and the withdrawal rate at 1.5 per cent, rather than the income threshold increasing to $67,000 and the withdrawal rate falling to 1 per cent from 2015–16.*"

Labor will oppose the bill at second reading but support it after government amendments remove the efficiency dividend and interest charge measures, while backing the conversion of student start-up scholarships to income-contingent loans and the removal of the HECS-HELP discount and voluntary repayment bonus, yielding $1.1 billion in budget savings.

The speaker supported converting student start-up scholarships into income-contingent loans (saving $920 million) and removing the HECS-HELP upfront payment discount and voluntary repayment bonus (saving $200 million), but opposed the efficiency dividend for higher education funding and imposing interest charges on debts like Abstudy and Austudy. The speaker argued these measures were originally proposed to fund the Gonski needs-based school funding model, which the government cut by $28 billion, and that the bill’s other measures represent an ideological attack on education, including introducing $100,000 university degrees.

The speaker argued that the Turnbull-Truss coalition government is a superior financial manager compared to the previous Labor government, citing a reduction in the budget deficit from $48 billion to $7 billion, a drop in unemployment from 6.2% to 5.9%, and 231,702 new jobs created. The speaker supported the Labor 2013-14 Budget Savings (Measures No. 2) Bill 2015, which includes an efficiency dividend for higher education grants and interest charges on unpaid Centrelink debts, and criticized Labor for wasteful spending and a lack of infrastructure projects in Western Australia.

The speech criticised the bill for adding $6,000 in average student debt and proposed fairer revenue measures, including ending the $2 billion diesel fuel rebate for miners, winding back superannuation tax concessions, or introducing a millionaire’s tax rate.

The speaker argued that Labor's 2013-14 Budget Savings Bill is needed to address Labor's $52 billion budget black hole, and criticised the Greens and Labor for blocking $17.2 billion in savings measures, including $2.1 billion in changes to student start-up scholarships and $1.2 billion in higher education efficiency dividends.
This bill would replace the current three-tier coastal shipping licence with a single permit that lasts 12 months and is available to both Australian and foreign vessels.

It would create minimum employment conditions for seafarers on foreign ships that carry coastal cargo for more than 183 days and require those ships to have two senior crew who are Australian citizens, residents or visa holders.

Vessels on the Australian International Shipping Register would no longer need to have a collective agreement before registration, and the requirement for them to mainly trade internationally would drop to 90 days a year.
Replaces the three-tier licensing system under the Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Act 2012 with a single Coastal Shipping Permit.
Renames the Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Act 2012 to the Coastal Shipping Act 2015.

Applies the Seagoing Industry Award to seafarers on foreign vessels with a coastal permit when the Fair Work Act 2009 covers them, and to Australian International Shipping Register vessels not trading internationally.
Creates an enforcement mechanism for seafarers to recover unpaid amounts if a foreign vessel trades for more than 183 days contrary to its permit.
Requires foreign vessels trading in coastal shipping for over 183 days to have two senior crew eligible to work in Australia as citizens, residents or visa holders.

Allows registration on the Australian International Shipping Register if a vessel engages in international shipping for 90 days or more a year, and removes the requirement for a collective agreement before registration.
Owners and operators of Australian and foreign vessels engaged in coastal shipping, seafarers on those vessels, and the Australian government.

The Shipping Legislation Amendment Bill 2015 simplifies coastal shipping regulation by replacing the existing tiered licensing system with a single 12-month permit for both Australian and foreign ships, aiming to reduce costs and increase competition. It notes that the Australian-flagged coastal fleet fell from 30 vessels in 2006-07 to 15 in 2013-14, and that shipping freight from Bell Bay Aluminium rose 63% from $18.20 to $29.70 per tonne in the first year of the 2012 Act.

The Shipping Legislation Amendment Bill 2015 was opposed for allowing foreign-flagged vessels paying lower wages to operate on Australian coastal routes, which the speaker argued would destroy Australian jobs, compromise maritime safety and national security, and harm the environment. The speaker moved an amendment to reject the bill and called for preserving Australian shipping industry protections.

The Shipping Legislation Amendment Bill 2015 aims to address the decline in Australia's coastal shipping industry, which the speaker attributes to the previous Labor government's Coastal Trading Act and union influence. The speaker cited a 63% increase in freight costs for Bell Bay Aluminium from 2011 to 2012, a drop in coastal freight loaded from over 59 million tonnes in 2007-08 to 49 million tonnes in 2012-13, and a decline in major Australian registered ships with coastal licences from 30 in 2006-07 to 13 by 2012-13.

The speaker opposed the Shipping Legislation Amendment Bill 2015, arguing it would strip Australian maritime workers of employment conditions and replace them with foreign crews, citing the case of the Alexander Spirit. They defended the 2012 Labor Coastal Trading Act reforms as providing a level playing field and warned the bill would risk the jobs of 2,000 seafarers and up to 8,000 land-based workers, attributing the government's push to ideological hostility toward unions like the Maritime Union of Australia.

Labor opposed the Shipping Legislation Amendment Bill 2015, arguing it would destroy Australian shipping jobs and reintroduce "Work Choices on water." The speaker claimed over 90% of shipping jobs were at risk, with the Australia Institute estimating only 88 Australian-employed seafarer jobs would remain if the bill passed.

The Assistant Minister to the Deputy Prime Minister argued that the Shipping Legislation Amendment Bill 2015 will deregulate coastal shipping by replacing the three-tiered licence system with a single permit for all ships, reducing costs and increasing competition. He cited specific figures including a 63% decline in the Australian coastal trading fleet's carrying capacity since 2012, a 63% increase in shipping freight rates for Bell Bay Aluminium under Labor's 2012 legislation, and claimed that 1,200 deaths at sea occurred under Labor's border protection policies.

The Shipping Legislation Amendment Bill is necessary reform that should be supported by both sides of the House, but the opposition will not support it due to obstructionism, while the government side will.

The speaker opposed the Shipping Legislation Amendment Bill 2015, arguing it would eliminate over 1,000 of 1,100 Australian shipping jobs and undermine wages, environmental protections, and national security, while defending Labor’s 2012 shipping reforms as a viable alternative.

The speaker opposed the Shipping Legislation Amendment Bill 2015, arguing it would replace 10,000 Australian jobs with foreign labour on flag-of-convenience vessels, undermine safety and environmental laws, and harm the Great Barrier Reef. The bill will replace the tiered permit system with a single permit for all ships, treat Australian and foreign vessels equally, and protect jobs by extending award entitlements to seafarers on foreign ships engaged in coastal shipping for over 183 days.

The member opposed the Shipping Legislation Amendment Bill 2015, arguing it would accelerate the loss of critical maritime skills (such as harbour masters and pilots) needed for efficient port operations, and noted that only 2% of Australian exports are carried by Australian-flagged ships. He cited a report by RMIT's Victor Gekara showing the decline of domiciled shipowners and training, and used Port Hedland's record of shipping 264,000 tonnes of iron ore in a single day as an example of the logistical capacity dependent on blue-water experience.

The speaker argued that the Shipping Legislation Amendment Bill 2015 would fix damage from Labor's 2012 coastal shipping laws, citing a 63% freight rate increase for Bell Bay Aluminium, a halving of the coastal trading fleet, and support from the Productivity Commission and Tasmanian business groups.

The speaker opposed the Shipping Legislation Amendment Bill 2015, arguing it would decimate Australian shipping and maritime jobs, citing 600 job losses at Forgacs in Newcastle and 10,000 direct/indirect jobs nationally. They claimed 88% of the bill's savings come from replacing Australian workers with 90% foreign crews, and referenced a Senate inquiry where a government official advised a cruise operator to sack Australian staff.

The speaker opposed the Shipping Legislation Amendment Bill 2015, arguing it would allow foreign vessels to access Australian coastal trade without paying Australian wages or observing safety standards, putting at least 2,000 direct maritime jobs at risk and potentially dismantling the domestic shipping industry. They supported amendments by the member for Grayndler and noted the government advised an Australian operator (Mr Milby of North Star Cruises) to register overseas and hire foreign workers.

The speaker supported the Shipping Legislation Amendment Bill 2015, arguing that previous Labor laws had failed and caused a 63% decline in coastal shipping carrying capacity, a 63% increase in freight costs for Bell Bay Aluminium, and a drop in Australian registered ships from 30 to 15. He also highlighted the need for efficient shipping to support free trade agreements and promoted the Bundaberg port as a potential site for a submarine maintenance base.

The Shipping Legislation Amendment Bill 2015 was condemned as a brutal attack on Australian workers, threatening 10,000 jobs and deregulating coastal shipping by allowing foreign flagged ships to operate for up to 183 days before being subject to Australian wage and conditions standards. The speaker argued the bill would reduce Australian seafarer jobs to just 88, replace Australian wages with Third World standards, and effectively reintroduce the Work Choices industrial relations system.

The Shipping Legislation Amendment Bill 2015 would replace Australian wage standards with foreign lower wages, with 88% of claimed savings from that replacement, and could reduce the Australian seafarer workforce from 1,177 to under 100. The speaker argued the bill should be rejected, noting that comparable nations like the US regulate coastal shipping and that the government's cost-benefit analysis ignored losses to Australian workers.

The speaker opposed the Shipping Legislation Amendment Bill 2015, arguing it would deregulate coastal shipping, remove preference for Australian-flagged and crewed vessels, and replace 10,000 Australian workers with foreign crews paid Third World wages—calling it "Work Choices on water" and noting that major trading partners like the US, Japan, Canada, and the EU protect their own coastal shipping.

The speaker argued that the Shipping Legislation Amendment Bill 2015 eliminates preference for Australian-flagged ships, establishes a single-permit system for foreign vessels, and deletes revitalising Australian shipping as a policy objective, with the Australia Institute estimating 93% of jobs will disappear and 88% of gains coming from replacing Australian workers. The speaker also cited examples of abandoned foreign-crewed ships and criticised the government's attitude toward job losses.

The speaker argued that the Shipping Legislation Amendment Bill 2015 would remove support for the Australian shipping industry, erode worker protections, and replace Australian seafarers with foreign crews at lower wages, citing that 88% of projected savings come from replacing Australian workers with 90% foreign crews. The speech also highlighted that shipping carries 99% of Australia's trade and employs 10,000 Australian workers.

The speech argued against the Shipping Legislation Amendment Bill 2015, claiming 88% of projected savings would come from replacing Australian workers with foreign crews and that the bill would undermine seafarer training and environmental protections for areas like the Great Barrier Reef, citing incidents involving the MV Pacific Adventurer and MV Shen Neng1.

The speaker opposed the Shipping Legislation Amendment Bill 2015, arguing it would cost 230 jobs in Tasmania and deter SeaRoad’s $100 million vessel investment, and called for scrapping the bill in favour of policies to expand the Australian flagged fleet, such as a Jones Act equivalent.

The speaker argued that the Shipping Legislation Amendment Bill 2015 should be withdrawn, claiming it would destroy Australian maritime jobs by allowing foreign-flagged, lower-wage vessels to replace Australian-flagged ships. They cited a decline in Australian-flagged vessels from 55 in 1996 to 13 currently, and referenced the Jones Act in the United States as a model for protecting domestic shipping and jobs.

The speaker opposed the Shipping Legislation Amendment Bill 2015, arguing it would deregulate Australian shipping, sacrifice national sovereignty, and repeat the mistakes documented in the bipartisan 1992 Ships of Shame report—which warned against lowering standards to flags of convenience. They claimed 88 per cent of the bill’s regulatory savings come from Australian seafarers’ wages and conditions.
National Disability Insurance Scheme Amendment Bill 2016

The speech supported the NDIS Amendment Bill 2016 but criticised the Western Australian government for choosing the WA model without an independent evaluation, calling on Minister Porter to bring WA into line. It also argued for a no-fault vaccine injury compensation scheme, citing the Hammond family and proposing a levy on pharmaceutical companies similar to the US model in place since 1987.

The Northern Australia Infrastructure Facility Bill 2016 provides $5 billion in concessional loans for northern infrastructure but is unfair to Western Australia, as its definition of "northern Australia" includes areas below the Tropic of Capricorn in Queensland and the Northern Territory but not in Western Australia. The speaker urged an amendment to use the 26th parallel for Western Australia, which would allow Carnarvon and Shark Bay to qualify.
Transport Security Amendment (Serious or Organised Crime) Bill 2016

The Labor speaker supported the Transport Security Amendment (Serious or Organised Crime) Bill but argued it is undermined by the government's visa policies, which allow poorly paid foreign workers with minimal checks into Australian ports, citing 7,732 overseas vessels in six months with only about 2,500 inspected, and a jump in 400 visa grants from 6,000 in 2012–13 to 54,688 in 2014–15.
Migration Amendment (Character Cancellation Consequential Provisions) Bill 2016

The speaker argued that the 12-month imprisonment trigger for mandatory visa cancellation under the character test is too sensitive, citing the case of a 53-year-old man who lived in Australia since infancy, had a psychotic episode, served his sentence, and was detained before his visa was restored. He called for a review of the triggers to balance community safety with reasonableness, especially for long-term residents.
Competition and Consumer Amendment (Payment Surcharges) Bill 2015

The speaker supported the Competition and Consumer Amendment (Payment Surcharges) Bill 2015, arguing for consumer protections against unexpectedly large credit card surcharges. They acknowledged the member for Hughes' faith in market competition but expressed concern about market failure and the concentration of power.
Australian Citizenship Amendment (Allegiance to Australia) Bill 2015

The speaker accepted the modified bill after its worst excesses were constrained by the joint committee, particularly Anthony Byrne and Mark Dreyfus, but flagged deep concerns about the legal fiction of self-actuating conduct and the threat to the separation of powers. He supported amendments targeting non-state participants like ISIS and convicted terrorists, while warning against unfettered ministerial power.
Australian Crime Commission Amendment (Criminology Research) Bill 2015

The Labor Party did not oppose the Australian Crime Commission Amendment (Criminology Research) Bill but expressed concerns that merging the Australian Institute of Criminology with the Australian Crime Commission would compromise independent research, risking the loss of data that could challenge law enforcement assumptions and hinder evidence-based policymaking.
Migration Amendment (Charging for a Migration Outcome) Bill 2015

The speaker supported the Migration Amendment (Charging for a Migration Outcome) Bill 2015 but argued it does not go far enough, warning that free trade agreements like KAFTA and ChAFTA allow jobs to be sold overseas without labour market testing, creating risks of indentured labour. They proposed amending the Migration Act to require registration in Australia for companies importing workers under contractual services arrangements, as current extraterritorial provisions would not reach foreign firms.
